98	  `own-blocked` means an amendment put a prerequisite under your own claim:
99	  post, print the board, hand back, and let your human partner remove the
100	  edge or let the prerequisite complete. `done`, `no-workspace` and `error`
101	  keep their handling: `done`: another session completed the task since you
102	  read the ledger; read its completion line, mark the task done, and never
103	  dispatch it. `no-workspace` (exit 2): the workspace is gone (finished or
104	  pruned elsewhere); stop, run `sync`, and re-read the ledger before
105	  anything else. `error` (exit 2, the same exit as `no-workspace` and a
106	  different problem): a read or a write failed, and the claim may already
107	  have been published; only your own retry of the same claim (which then
108	  answers `held own=1`) or a takeover clears it. Stop, show the stderr line,
109	  and retry the same claim once its cause is fixed; `sync` is still not the
110	  answer. Any other status stops the dispatch until `claim` succeeds; show
111	  its stderr line.
112	- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result in the
113	  ledger's task entry
114	  (`Task <N>: implementer <agent-id-or-name> (model <model>, session <sid>, worktree <path>, branch <name>)`) —
115	  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent where the harness has no foreground
116	  dispatch and dispatch on its recorded model where it does, and after compaction the ledger is
117	  the only place the identity survives once its agent has exited. An
118	  identity that was never written down forces a fresh takeover where a
119	  resume was owed.
120	- When another session may be live on this plan, append ledger lines with a
121	  quoted heredoc (`cat >> <workspace>/progress.md <<'EOF'`), never with the
122	  Edit tool, whose read-modify-write drops a line another session appended
123	  in between.
124	- Where the Agent tool offers `run_in_background`, dispatch with it false; where it does not (fork mode in an interactive terminal), dispatches run in the background and the stop guard treats them as live work.
125	
126	Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)
127	
128	### 2. Handle the report
129	
130	Append `Task <N>: report <status> <one line>` to the ledger when the report arrives, before acting on it.
131	
132	**Subagent Reports Are Claims.** Subagent reports are claims, not
133	evidence. Before acting on any completed-status report (DONE or DONE_WITH_CONCERNS) or a fix report —
134	dispatching the reviewer, re-running a gate, marking a task complete — the
135	controller re-runs the named covering test command directly and compares
136	the output against the report. A misreported result is a failed task:
137	re-dispatch with the discrepancy named, not a bookkeeping correction.
138	
139	Every implementer and fix dispatch names either its covering test
140	command(s) or an explicit `no covering command: <rationale>` line plus the
141	controller's substitute verification (read the diff against the brief;
142	render or grep the changed doc). A dispatch naming neither is malformed —
143	fix the dispatch, not the rule.
144	
145	A covering command must be able to fail. One that can no-op on the state
146	under test — a changed-files linter on a clean tree, a test filter that
147	matches nothing — is not covering evidence, however honestly it exits 0.
148	Name the files or the test ids explicitly so the command exercises what
149	the report claims.
150	
151	Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:
152	
153	**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints `wrote <path>: <N> commit(s), <N> bytes`, so take the path from that line; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task). If `review-package` exits non-zero, read its stderr and fix the range before dispatching — exit 2 means bad inputs (wrong argument count, a missing plan file, a ref that does not resolve) or an ancestry check git itself could not answer (a missing or corrupt object); exit 3 means BASE..HEAD is empty or HEAD is not a descendant of BASE, usually a wrong-branch commit; never dispatch a reviewer without a package. Otherwise, dispatch the task reviewer with the path: step 3, in [review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md).
154	
155	**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.
156	
157	**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.
158	
159	**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
160	1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
161	2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
162	3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
163	4. If the plan itself is wrong, stop and escalate to your human partner — the plan text, what it breaks, and the correction you would make
164	
165	**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.
166	
167	If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
168	clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
169	rush it into implementation.
170	
171

1	---
2	name: subagent-driven-development
3	description: Use when executing implementation plans with independent tasks in the current session
4	---
5	
6	# Subagent-Driven Development
7	
8	Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.
9	
10	**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.
11	
12	**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration
13	
14	**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
15	ledger and the tool results carry the record.
16	
17	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for anything you write to your human partner in this skill: the pre-flight question, an escalation, a BLOCKED hand-back.
18	
19	**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. While the plan has tasks left, a turn ends in exactly three cases: a BLOCKED status you cannot resolve; a question only your human partner can answer, asked in that message (ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress is such a question); or, on a harness that cannot wait in the foreground, tracked work still running, named in that message. A message that names your next step is followed by that step's tool call in the same turn. "Tasks 1 and 2 are done. Moving to Task 3." followed by a turn end is a stop: your human partner reads it as work in progress, and nothing resumes it until they type. Completing the last task does not end the plan: it opens the final whole-branch review, and the plan ends only after Finish. Each permitted turn end, and "your human partner asked you to stop", is written to the ledger in the same message that ends the turn: run `scripts/sdd-state handback PLAN_FILE --reason "<why>"` (add `--session <sid>` on a harness without `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`; `busy` or `error` is retried, and without the line the guard falls back to reading your last message). Write that line only for a question only your human partner can answer, a BLOCKED report, or their request to stop; finishing the tasks is never a reason for it. On Claude Code the SDD stop guard refuses a turn end it can prove is premature, two consecutive attempts per plan, the count resetting after any allow, with this message: "SDD stop guard: plan <plan path> is not finished (<state>; nothing tracked is live). Take the next step now, in this turn. If you are handing back to your human partner (a question only they can answer, a BLOCKED report, or they asked you to stop), run scripts/sdd-state handback PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --reason "<why>" and end the turn with that message." (with a live job the first sentences name the job and say to watch it with `tracked-job wait`). When you meet it, take the next step; writing a question you do not need answered to get past it is the stop it exists to prevent, and the log records every allow. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.
20	
21	**Tracked work only:** anything that outlives one tool call starts through your harness's tracked background option (`run_in_background` on Claude Code); never start it with a trailing `&`, `nohup`, `setsid`, `disown`, or a script that detaches a process. The harness never reports on such a process, so nothing wakes you when it ends, and a turn you end to wait for it does not resume.
22	
23	**After every context compaction:** this file fits within the 20,000 characters Claude Code re-attaches, so the copy you hold is whole. A step file you read before the compaction does not survive it. Before your next action, print the board and the ledger lines the step table names (your task's and your Setup's, never the whole ledger), find your step in the table, and Read that step file in full.
24	
25	## When to Use
26	
27	```dot
28	digraph when_to_use {
29	    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
30	    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
31	    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
32	    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
33	    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
34	    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];
35	
36	    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
37	    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
38	    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
39	    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
40	    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
41	    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
42	}
43	```
44	
45	**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
46	- Same session (no context switch)
47	- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
48	- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
49	- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)
50	
51	## The Process
52	
53	Each step's full text is in its own file beside this one. Read a step's file when you enter the step; after a compaction, the step table below names the one to read.
54	
55	1. **Setup** ([setup.md](setup.md)): sync the state branch and find the plan's workspace, settle where the work happens (hyperpowers:using-git-worktrees), create or read the ledger and append your session line, verify, read the plan and the spec, run the pre-flight scan. Setup's last action appends `session <sid>: setup complete`.
56	2. **Take a task and dispatch** ([task-loop.md](task-loop.md)): `scripts/sdd-state next` offers a task; claim the first and switch to its branch (none to take, or blocked: post, print the board, hand back). Dispatch the implementer, answer its questions, handle its report.
57	3. **Review the task** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): generate the review package and dispatch the task reviewer. Blocking findings go to step 4; a finding that conflicts with the plan text goes to your human partner first.
58	4. **Fix loop** ([fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md)): fix rounds, each with a scoped re-review, under the shared cap in the rules below. When no finding is left open, go back to review-and-complete.md for the gate.
59	5. **Codex task gate and completion** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): unless the task's effective tier is low, run the per-task Codex gate (blocking findings re-enter step 4). Append the `approved` line, merge back, detach, delete the task branch, and run `scripts/sdd-state complete`; any status but `complete` stops. Then step 2.
60	6. **Final review and Finish** ([final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md)): when no task remains, claim the final train, dispatch the final reviewer (one fix dispatch, one scoped re-review), the decision extractor and the Codex final gate, delete the workspace, then use hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.
61	
62	## After a compaction: the step table
63	
64	Print the board (`scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE`) and the ledger lines of your task and your Setup (`grep -E '^(Task <N>:|session <sid>: setup complete)' <workspace>/progress.md`, leaving out `Task <N>:` when you hold no task); `scripts/sdd-dir PLAN_FILE` prints the workspace. Do not Read the whole ledger after a compaction: it grows with the plan. A row's newest line is the newest of your task's lines the table names (its branch, base, implementer identity, `report`, `review`, Codex gate round, `approved`, `merged` and `fix round` lines); a line it does not name, such as a deferred minor or the gate directory, leaves your step unchanged. Then Read the step file this table names:
65	
66	| State | Step file |
67	|---|---|
68	| no ledger in the workspace, or no `setup complete` line of this session in it | [setup.md](setup.md) |
69	| the board shows no task held by this session and a task without a completion line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
70	| the held task's newest line is its branch, base, implementer identity or `report` line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
71	| its newest line is a `review` or Codex gate line approving it, an `approved` line or a `merged` line | [review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md) |
72	| its newest line is a `fix round` line, or a `review` or Codex gate line with blocking findings | [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) |
73	| this session holds the final claim, or every task has a completion line | [final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md) |
74	
75	A state the table does not cover reads [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), and you record that in the ledger.
76	
77	The table reads these ledger lines, so write each one where its step says:
78	
79	- `session <sid>: setup complete`, Setup's last action;
80	- `Task <N>: report <status> <one line>`, after an implementer's report;
81	- `Task <N>: review <approved|blocking> <reviewer id> <one line>`, after a task review or scoped re-review;
82	- `Task <N>: codex gate round <R> <approved|blocking> <one line>`, after each per-task Codex gate round.
83	
84	## Rules for every step
85	
86	These hold in every step file. Where a step file and this section differ, this section governs.
87	
88	- Tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE — do not re-dispatch them. Conversation memory does not survive compaction. After compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
89	- Dispatch implementer, task-reviewer, fix-round, re-review and final-reviewer subagents with `run_in_background: false`. Your next step always depends on the result, and a foreground call keeps your turn open, which is what an editor such as Zed shows as the session working. A background dispatch ends the turn while the subagent runs, and the editor shows the session idle.
90	- Run a covering command expected to finish within 10 minutes in the foreground, with an explicit timeout of at least its expected runtime and at most 600000 ms. A command that may run past 10 minutes is a tracked job; [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), "Waiting on subagents and long commands", gives its commands and watch budget.
91	- One implementer at a time in this session: parallel work is other sessions' (one controller per task branch); never dispatch two implementers at once here.
92	- Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review. The one exception is the de-minimis fix in [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md).
93	- The task reviewer's blocking findings and the per-task Codex gate's blocking findings form one loop with ONE shared cap of **five rounds per task**: the gate does not run a count of its own.
94	- When round 5's re-review — or a per-task Codex gate at the spent cap — still leaves blocking findings open, stop dispatching and surface the task as BLOCKED, as [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) describes under the breaker.
95	
96	## Model Selection
97	
98	Match the model to the task's difficulty rather than defaulting. Two rules are
99	defaults you will get wrong by omission, so they stay here: **always specify
100	the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent** — an omitted model inherits
101	your session's, usually the most capable and most expensive — and **a mid-tier
102	model is the floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose
103	descriptions**, whatever the schedule pressure. The cheapest tier is for
104	transcription, where the task's own text carries the complete code to write,
105	and for single-file mechanical fixes. The per-role guidance, the complexity
106	signals, and the fix-loop escalation rule are in
107	[model-selection.md](model-selection.md).
108	
109	## The waiting board
110	
111	Before you ask your human partner a question, hand back BLOCKED, meet an
112	empty frontier (`held` or `blocked`), or stop on a merge conflict, post what
113	you wait on: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --kind
114	<question|tasks|merge|gate|handoff> [--task N] --note "<one line>"`, and put
115	the session lines of `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE` in what you write.
116	When you resume, clear it: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --clear`.
117	The board is how your human partner finds the session that needs them among
118	several; a session that holds a claim and posts nothing shows as quiet
119	after half an hour, which is where they look for a permission prompt.
120	
121	## Risk Tiers (per-task Codex gate applicability)
122	
123	Tiers are `low`, `standard`, `high`, declared per task in the plan. A task
124	skips the per-task Codex gate only when all three hold: declared low, the
125	plan's own Codex gate actually reviewed the plan, and no escalation trigger
126	fired at any point during execution. That skip is recorded durably. An
127	unreviewed low tier — plan gate skipped, degraded, or outcome unknown —
128	executes as standard, and a task demoted that way runs the full train and
129	records NO tier-skip event. The Claude task reviewer and the final
130	whole-branch train never tier off. When any task did skip, write
131	`tier-skips.md` in this plan's workspace; Final Review hands its path to the

5	**Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are

7	constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch
8	one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and
9	its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff
10	as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own

12	A batch's effective risk tier for the per-task Codex gate is the MAX of the
13	batched tasks' declared tiers — batching low-tier tasks never manufactures
14	a gate skip.

16	Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
17	prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
18	and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

20	**Waiting on subagents and long commands.** SKILL.md (Rules for every step) sets the foreground rule; a tracked job runs this way:
21	
22	- Allocate a tracked job in the foreground with `scripts/tracked-job new PLAN_FILE <name> --budget-ms <budget>` (the watch budget below; the helper writes the `jobdir=` line in the ledger itself), launch `scripts/tracked-job run <jobdir> -- <command>` through the tracked background option with the budget as its timeout, then watch it in the foreground with repeated `scripts/tracked-job wait <jobdir> --max-ms 600000` calls: `exited code=0` is success; any other `exited` code is a failed command, handled as that command's failure (a failed test is a fix round, a failed covering command a failed task); `running` at the bound means another `wait`; on `lost`, run `tracked-job stop <jobdir>` first and read its answer before you go on: only `stopped` or `not-running` means the survivors are swept and the job can be treated as failed (a process in the job's group that carried no fence is left alone and counted as `skipped` in `<jobdir>/meta.json`, and one that outlived the KILL is counted in `survivors`; report a nonzero `survivors` or `skipped`, or a record you cannot read, to your human partner with the jobdir and pgid before you go on, and never call that job stopped); `busy` means the lock was held and nothing was swept, so run `stop` again; `status=error` means the job directory could not be read, so escalate it to your human partner naming the jobdir and leave the job live; `lost-unswept pgid=<n>` means the sweep needs a shell that can list processes and read their identity (the sandbox cannot), so the job stays live to the stop guard until `tracked-job stop <jobdir>` runs where it can: report it to your human partner with its pgid beside the failure, and expect a reused pid to read as `running` until that sweep. When you need a job's output, write the tail of its `out.log` to `<workspace>/reports/job-<name>.txt` and cite the path; output never goes in the ledger. A background shell you start in a turn without `tracked-job` is live work no job record names: end the turn while one is still running and the stop guard refuses that turn end as `live-shell`. Codex reviews already follow this shape through the recipe's `status <job-id> --wait --json` loop.
23	- **Watch budget.** The total watch on one job is three times the plan's stated runtime for it, or 60 minutes when the plan states none, capped at the harness's maximum background lifetime (7200000 ms on Claude Code). The watch ends when `wait` reports `exited`, `lost` or `lost-unswept`; a supervisor the harness killed writes no exit file, and `wait` reports it as `lost`. When the budget is spent with the job still running, run `tracked-job stop <jobdir>` and read its answer before you end the turn: `stopped` or `not-running` means the job is over, so write the `out.log` tail to `<workspace>/reports/job-<name>.txt` and report BLOCKED naming that path (a nonzero `survivors` or `skipped` in `<jobdir>/meta.json`, or a record you cannot read, is reported the same way, with the jobdir and pgid, and that job is never called stopped); `busy` means the workspace lock was held and nothing changed, so run `stop` again; `stop-timeout` means the supervisor has not concluded the job, so run `stop` again, three calls in all, and escalate a third one to your human partner as a job still live, naming the jobdir; `status=error` means the job directory could not be read, so escalate it the same way, naming the jobdir; `lost-unswept pgid=<n>` leaves the job live, so report it to your human partner as still live with its pgid, never as stopped.
24	
25	On a harness whose subagents run asynchronously, never poll a wait interface with short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either. While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review, reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own. When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session. 128	### 2. Handle the report
129	
130	Append `Task <N>: report <status> <one line>` to the ledger when the report arrives, before acting on it.
131	
132	**Subagent Reports Are Claims.** Subagent reports are claims, not
133	evidence. Before acting on any completed-status report (DONE or DONE_WITH_CONCERNS) or a fix report —
134	dispatching the reviewer, re-running a gate, marking a task complete — the
135	controller re-runs the named covering test command directly and compares
136	the output against the report. A misreported result is a failed task:
137	re-dispatch with the discrepancy named, not a bookkeeping correction.
138	
139	Every implementer and fix dispatch names either its covering test
140	command(s) or an explicit `no covering command: <rationale>` line plus the
141	controller's substitute verification (read the diff against the brief;
142	render or grep the changed doc). A dispatch naming neither is malformed —
143	fix the dispatch, not the rule.
144	
145	A covering command must be able to fail. One that can no-op on the state
146	under test — a changed-files linter on a clean tree, a test filter that
147	matches nothing — is not covering evidence, however honestly it exits 0.
148	Name the files or the test ids explicitly so the command exercises what
149	the report claims.
150	
151	Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:
152	
153	**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints `wrote <path>: <N> commit(s), <N> bytes`, so take the path from that line; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task). Otherwise, dispatch the task reviewer with the path: step 3, in [review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md).
154	
155	**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.
156	
157	**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.
158	
159	**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
160	1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
161	2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
162	3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
163	4. If the plan itself is wrong, stop and escalate to your human partner — the plan text, what it breaks, and the correction you would make
164	
165	**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.
166	
167	If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
168	clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
169	rush it into implementation.

6	# Subagent-Driven Development

8	Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.
9	
10	**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

17	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for anything you write to your human partner in this skill: the pre-flight question, an escalation, a BLOCKED hand-back.
18	
19	**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. While the plan has tasks left, a turn ends in exactly three cases: a BLOCKED status you cannot resolve; a question only your human partner can answer, asked in that message (ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress is such a question); or, on a harness that cannot wait in the foreground, tracked work still running, named in that message. A message that names your next step is followed by that step's tool call in the same turn. "Tasks 1 and 2 are done. Moving to Task 3." followed by a turn end is a stop: your human partner reads it as work in progress, and nothing resumes it until they type. Completing the last task does not end the plan: it opens the final whole-branch review, and the plan ends only after Finish. Each permitted turn end, and "your human partner asked you to stop", is written to the ledger in the same message that ends the turn: run `scripts/sdd-state handback PLAN_FILE --reason "<why>"` (add `--session <sid>` on a harness without `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`; `busy` or `error` is retried, and without the line the guard falls back to reading your last message). Write that line only for a question only your human partner can answer, a BLOCKED report, or their request to stop; finishing the tasks is never a reason for it. On Claude Code the SDD stop guard refuses a turn end it can prove is premature, two consecutive attempts per plan, the count resetting after any allow, with this message: "SDD stop guard: plan <plan path> is not finished (<state>; nothing tracked is live). Take the next step now, in this turn. If you are handing back to your human partner (a question only they can answer, a BLOCKED report, or they asked you to stop), run scripts/sdd-state handback PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --reason "<why>" and end the turn with that message." (with a live job the first sentences name the job and say to watch it with `tracked-job wait`). 57	3. **Review the task** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): generate the review package and dispatch the task reviewer. Blocking findings go to step 4; a finding that conflicts with the plan text goes to your human partner first.
58	4. **Fix loop** ([fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md)): fix rounds, each with a scoped re-review, under the shared cap in the rules below. When no finding is left open, go back to review-and-complete.md for the gate.
59	5. **Codex task gate and completion** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): unless the task's effective tier is low, run the per-task Codex gate (blocking findings re-enter step 4). Append the `approved` line, merge back, detach, delete the task branch, and run `scripts/sdd-state complete`; any status but `complete` stops. Then step 2.
60	6. **Final review and Finish** ([final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md)): when no task remains, claim the final train, dispatch the final reviewer (one fix dispatch, one scoped re-review), the decision extractor and the Codex final gate, delete the workspace, then use hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.
61	
62	## After a compaction: the step table
63	
64	Print the board (`scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE`) and the ledger lines of your task and your Setup (`grep -E '^(Task <N>:|session <sid>: setup complete)' <workspace>/progress.md`, leaving out `Task <N>:` when you hold no task); `scripts/sdd-dir PLAN_FILE` prints the workspace. Do not Read the whole ledger after a compaction: it grows with the plan. A row's newest line is the newest of your task's lines the table names (its branch, base, implementer identity, `report`, `review`, Codex gate round, `approved`, `merged` and `fix round` lines); a line it does not name, such as a deferred minor or the gate directory, leaves your step unchanged. Then Read the step file this table names:
65	
66	| State | Step file |
67	|---|---|
68	| no ledger in the workspace, or no `setup complete` line of this session in it | [setup.md](setup.md) |
69	| the board shows no task held by this session and a task without a completion line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
70	| the held task's newest line is its branch, base, implementer identity or `report` line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
71	| its newest line is a `review` or Codex gate line approving it, an `approved` line or a `merged` line | [review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md) |
72	| its newest line is a `fix round` line, or a `review` or Codex gate line with blocking findings | [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) |
73	| this session holds the final claim, or every task has a completion line | [final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md) |
74	
75	A state the table does not cover reads [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), and you record that in the ledger.
76	
77	The table reads these ledger lines, so write each one where its step says:
78	
79	- `session <sid>: setup complete`, Setup's last action;
80	- `Task <N>: report <status> <one line>`, after an implementer's report;
81	- `Task <N>: review <approved|blocking> <reviewer id> <one line>`, after a task review or scoped re-review;
82	- `Task <N>: codex gate round <R> <approved|blocking> <one line>`, after each per-task Codex gate round.
83	
84	## Rules for every step
85	
86	These hold in every step file. Where a step file and this section differ, this section governs.
87	
88	- Tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE — do not re-dispatch them. Conversation memory does not survive compaction. After compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
89	- Dispatch implementer, task-reviewer, fix-round, re-review and final-reviewer subagents with `run_in_background: false`. Your next step always depends on the result, and a foreground call keeps your turn open, which is what an editor such as Zed shows as the session working. A background dispatch ends the turn while the subagent runs, and the editor shows the session idle.
90	- Run a covering command expected to finish within 10 minutes in the foreground, with an explicit timeout of at least its expected runtime and at most 600000 ms. A command that may run past 10 minutes is a tracked job; [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), "Waiting on subagents and long commands", gives its commands and watch budget.
91	- One implementer at a time in this session: parallel work is other sessions' (one controller per task branch); never dispatch two implementers at once here.
92	- Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review. The one exception is the de-minimis fix in [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md).
93	- The task reviewer's blocking findings and the per-task Codex gate's blocking findings form one loop with ONE shared cap of **five rounds per task**: the gate does not run a count of its own.
94	- When round 5's re-review — or a per-task Codex gate at the spent cap — still leaves blocking findings open, stop dispatching and surface the task as BLOCKED, as [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) describes under the breaker.
95	
96	## Model Selection
97	
98	Match the model to the task's difficulty rather than defaulting. Two rules are
99	defaults you will get wrong by omission, so they stay here: **always specify
100	the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent** — an omitted model inherits
101	your session's, usually the most capable and most expensive — and **a mid-tier
102	model is the floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose
103	descriptions**, whatever the schedule pressure. The cheapest tier is for
104	transcription, where the task's own text carries the complete code to write,
105	and for single-file mechanical fixes. The per-role guidance, the complexity
106	signals, and the fix-loop escalation rule are in
107	[model-selection.md](model-selection.md).
108	
109	## The waiting board
110	
111	Before you ask your human partner a question, hand back BLOCKED, meet an
112	empty frontier (`held` or `blocked`), or stop on a merge conflict, post what
113	you wait on: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --kind
114	<question|tasks|merge|gate|handoff> [--task N] --note "<one line>"`, and put
115	the session lines of `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE` in what you write.
116	When you resume, clear it: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --clear`.
117	The board is how your human partner finds the session that needs them among
118	several; a session that holds a claim and posts nothing shows as quiet
119	after half an hour, which is where they look for a permission prompt.
120	
121	## Risk Tiers (per-task Codex gate applicability)
122	
123	Tiers are `low`, `standard`, `high`, declared per task in the plan. A task
124	skips the per-task Codex gate only when all three hold: declared low, the
125	plan's own Codex gate actually reviewed the plan, and no escalation trigger
126	fired at any point during execution. That skip is recorded durably. An
127	unreviewed low tier — plan gate skipped, degraded, or outcome unknown —
128	executes as standard, and a task demoted that way runs the full train and
129	records NO tier-skip event. The Claude task reviewer and the final
130	whole-branch train never tier off. When any task did skip, write
131	`tier-skips.md` in this plan's workspace; Final Review hands its path to the
132	final reviewer and the final Codex gate. The escalation triggers, the
133	fallback rules, and the exact ledger line shape are in
134	[risk-tiers.md](risk-tiers.md) — read it before dispatching any task declared
135	low.
136	
137	## Common Rationalizations
138	
139	The excuses that show up mid-run and what is actually true:
140	[common-rationalizations.md](common-rationalizations.md). Read it the moment you
141	catch yourself justifying a shortcut.
142	
143	## Example Workflow
144	
145	A complete worked run, dispatch through finish:
146	[example-workflow.md](example-workflow.md).

results.content:
1	## The Task Loop
2	
3	Part of [SKILL.md](SKILL.md); the rules there hold in this step.
4	
5	**Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are
6	each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix,
7	constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch
8	one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and
9	its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff
10	as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own
11	judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface.
12	A batch's effective risk tier for the per-task Codex gate is the MAX of the
13	batched tasks' declared tiers — batching low-tier tasks never manufactures
14	a gate skip.
15	
16	Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
17	prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
18	and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.
19	
20	**Waiting on subagents and long commands.** SKILL.md (Rules for every step) sets the foreground rule; a tracked job runs this way:
21	
22	- Allocate a tracked job in the foreground with `scripts/tracked-job new PLAN_FILE <name> --budget-ms <budget>` (the watch budget below; the helper writes the `jobdir=` line in the ledger itself), launch `scripts/tracked-job run <jobdir> -- <command>` through the tracked background option with the budget as its timeout, then watch it in the foreground with repeated `scripts/tracked-job wait <jobdir> --max-ms 600000` calls: `exited code=0` is success; any other `exited` code is a failed command, handled as that command's failure (a failed test is a fix round, a failed covering command a failed task); `running` at the bound means another `wait`; on `lost`, run `tracked-job stop <jobdir>` first and read its answer before you go on: only `stopped` or `not-running` means the survivors are swept and the job can be treated as failed (a process in the job's group that carried no fence is left alone and counted as `skipped` in `<jobdir>/meta.json`, and one that outlived the KILL is counted in `survivors`; report a nonzero `survivors` or `skipped`, or a record you cannot read, to your human partner with the jobdir and pgid before you go on, and never call that job stopped); `busy` means the lock was held and nothing was swept, so run `stop` again; `status=error` means the job directory could not be read, so escalate it to your human partner naming the jobdir and leave the job live; `lost-unswept pgid=<n>` means the sweep needs a shell that can list processes and read their identity (the sandbox cannot), so the job stays live to the stop guard until `tracked-job stop <jobdir>` runs where it can: report it to your human partner with its pgid beside the failure, and expect a reused pid to read as `running` until that sweep. When you need a job's output, write the tail of its `out.log` to `<workspace>/reports/job-<name>.txt` and cite the path; output never goes in the ledger. A background shell you start in a turn without `tracked-job` is live work no job record names: end the turn while one is still running and the stop guard refuses that turn end as `live-shell`. Codex reviews already follow this shape through the recipe's `status <job-id> --wait --json` loop.
23	- **Watch budget.** The total watch on one job is three times the plan's stated runtime for it, or 60 minutes when the plan states none, capped at the harness's maximum background lifetime (7200000 ms on Claude Code). The watch ends when `wait` reports `exited`, `lost` or `lost-unswept`; a supervisor the harness killed writes no exit file, and `wait` reports it as `lost`. When the budget is spent with the job still running, run `tracked-job stop <jobdir>` and read its answer before you end the turn: `stopped` or `not-running` means the job is over, so write the `out.log` tail to `<workspace>/reports/job-<name>.txt` and report BLOCKED naming that path (a nonzero `survivors` or `skipped` in `<jobdir>/meta.json`, or a record you cannot read, is reported the same way, with the jobdir and pgid, and that job is never called stopped); `busy` means the workspace lock was held and nothing changed, so run `stop` again; `stop-timeout` means the supervisor has not concluded the job, so run `stop` again, three calls in all, and escalate a third one to your human partner as a job still live, naming the jobdir; `status=error` means the job directory could not be read, so escalate it the same way, naming the jobdir; `lost-unswept pgid=<n>` leaves the job live, so report it to your human partner as still live with its pgid, never as stopped.
24	
25	On a harness whose subagents run asynchronously, never poll a wait interface with short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either. While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review, reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own. When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session. Codex's `wait_agent` blocks inside the turn; `using-hyperpowers/references/codex-tools.md` maps it.
26	
27	### 1. Dispatch the implementer
28	
29	Record BASE right after `git switch <branch>` and before dispatching, as the
30	task branch's fork point from the integration branch:
31	`git merge-base HEAD refs/heads/<integration branch>` (the full ref name, so
32	a tag with the branch's name cannot be read instead). On a fresh claim that
33	is the claim's `from=` commit. On a takeover it is the original claim's base,
34	or, once the conflict route has merged the integration branch into the task
35	branch, the integration head merged in; the previous holder's commits stay in
36	the review package and the fix-round diffs either way, which both need BASE.
37	A HEAD read before the claim can lag the integration branch while other
38	sessions merge.
39	
40	- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
41	  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
42	  uniquely named file and prints `wrote <path>: <N> lines`. Take the path
43	  from that line; do not paste the line itself into a dispatch. Compose the
44	  dispatch so the
45	  brief stays the single source of
46	  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
47	  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
48	  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
49	  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
50	  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
51	  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
52	  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
53	  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
54	- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
55	  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
56	  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
57	  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
58	- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
59	  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
60	  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
61	  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
62	  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
63	- The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the
64	  implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents —
65	  not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the
66	  report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated
67	  the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra
68	  review seat per task.
69	- Subagents follow hyperpowers:test-driven-development for the task's tests.
70	- If an earlier task deferred a finding in the area this task touches — a
71	  Minor in the ledger, or one your human partner decided — carry a pointer
72	  to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
73	- Ask what to take: `scripts/sdd-state next PLAN_FILE --session <sid>`.
74	  `status=next tasks=<list>` names the claimable tasks in plan order, this
75	  session's own claims first; claim the first:
76	  `scripts/sdd-state claim PLAN_FILE N --session <sid>`. `claimed` prints the
77	  task branch and its base: check the branch out (`git switch <branch>`) and
78	  dispatch on it; `held` with your own session id (`own=1`, a resume after
79	  compaction) prints the same two fields: check the branch out and proceed;
80	  `held` with `own=1` and `merged=1` means the task is already merged and its
81	  branch deleted: check nothing out and resume it at its completion line
82	  (Complete the task, in [review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)); `claimed` with `takeover=1` and `merged=1`
83	  means the same after a takeover: the task is already merged, so check
84	  nothing out, dispatch nothing, and resume it at its completion line (the
85	  previous holder's task branch may still exist; you do not need it);
86	  `held` from `claim` after `next` offered the task is a race lost, run
87	  `next` again; `blocked` means the plan moved under you, run `next` again.
88	  A task held by another session is ordinary while next offers another: take
89	  what it offers. When `next` prints `status=none reason=<reason>`:
90	  `complete` goes to the final train (Finish, in [final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md)); `assigned-complete` is
91	  reported and the session hands back; `held` and `blocked` mean post a
92	  waiting record (`scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --kind
93	  tasks --note "<the held= and waiting= fields>"`), print
94	  `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE`, and hand back with the board's session
95	  lines in your message. Take a held task over only on your human partner's
96	  explicit yes to a question that names the holder and the time since
97	  (`--takeover`), recording the takeover beside the original identity;
98	  `own-blocked` means an amendment put a prerequisite under your own claim:
99	  post, print the board, hand back, and let your human partner remove the
100	  edge or let the prerequisite complete. `done`, `no-workspace` and `error`
101	  keep their handling: `done`: another session completed the task since you
102	  read the ledger; read its completion line, mark the task done, and never
103	  dispatch it. `no-workspace` (exit 2): the workspace is gone (finished or
104	  pruned elsewhere); stop, run `sync`, and re-read the ledger before
105	  anything else. `error` (exit 2, the same exit as `no-workspace` and a
106	  different problem): a read or a write failed, and the claim may already
107	  have been published; only your own retry of the same claim (which then
108	  answers `held own=1`) or a takeover clears it. Stop, show the stderr line,
109	  and retry the same claim once its cause is fixed; `sync` is still not the
110	  answer. Any other status stops the dispatch until `claim` succeeds; show
111	  its stderr line.
112	- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result in the
113	  ledger's task entry
114	  (`Task <N>: implementer <agent-id-or-name> (model <model>, session <sid>, worktree <path>, branch <name>)`) —
115	  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent where the harness has no foreground
116	  dispatch and dispatch on its recorded model where it does, and after compaction the ledger is
117	  the only place the identity survives once its agent has exited. An
118	  identity that was never written down forces a fresh takeover where a
119	  resume was owed.
120	- When another session may be live on this plan, append ledger lines with a
121	  quoted heredoc (`cat >> <workspace>/progress.md <<'EOF'`), never with the
122	  Edit tool, whose read-modify-write drops a line another session appended
123	  in between.
124	- Where the Agent tool offers `run_in_background`, dispatch with it false; where it does not (fork mode in an interactive terminal), dispatches run in the background and the stop guard treats them as live work.
125	
126	Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)
127	
128	### 2. Handle the report
129	
130	Append `Task <N>: report <status> <one line>` to the ledger when the report arrives, before acting on it.
131	
132	**Subagent Reports Are Claims.** Subagent reports are claims, not
133	evidence. Before acting on any completed-status report (DONE or DONE_WITH_CONCERNS) or a fix report —
134	dispatching the reviewer, re-running a gate, marking a task complete — the
135	controller re-runs the named covering test command directly and compares
136	the output against the report. A misreported result is a failed task:
137	re-dispatch with the discrepancy named, not a bookkeeping correction.
138	
139	Every implementer and fix dispatch names either its covering test
140	command(s) or an explicit `no covering command: <rationale>` line plus the
141	controller's substitute verification (read the diff against the brief;
142	render or grep the changed doc). A dispatch naming neither is malformed —
143	fix the dispatch, not the rule.
144	
145	A covering command must be able to fail. One that can no-op on the state
146	under test — a changed-files linter on a clean tree, a test filter that
147	matches nothing — is not covering evidence, however honestly it exits 0.
148	Name the files or the test ids explicitly so the command exercises what
149	the report claims.
150	
151	Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:
152	
153	**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints `wrote <path>: <N> commit(s), <N> bytes`, so take the path from that line; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task). If `review-package` exits non-zero, read its stderr and fix the range before dispatching — exit 2 means bad inputs (wrong argument count, a missing plan file, a ref that does not resolve) or an ancestry check git itself could not answer (a missing or corrupt object); exit 3 means BASE..HEAD is empty or HEAD is not a descendant of BASE, usually a wrong-branch commit; never dispatch a reviewer without a package. Otherwise, dispatch the task reviewer with the path: step 3, in [review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md).
154	
155	**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.
156	
157	**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.
158	
159	**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
160	1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
161	2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
162	3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
163	4. If the plan itself is wrong, stop and escalate to your human partner — the plan text, what it breaks, and the correction you would make
164	
165	**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.
166	
167	If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
168	clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
169	rush it into implementation.
170

1	# Global constraints (verbatim from plan.md: Architecture, Tech Stack, Conventions)
2	
3	**Architecture:** One CommonJS module, `src/textstats.js`, exports four pure functions. A private `tokenize` helper (added in Task 1) is the single definition of what a "word" is; `wordCount`, `topWords` and `readingTimeMinutes` all build on it so the three numbers can never disagree about the text. `sentenceCount` (Task 2) uses its own terminator scan and borrows `tokenize` only to decide whether a segment holds any words at all. Every function validates its arguments and throws a `TypeError` or `RangeError` with a message naming the function, rather than returning a silent wrong answer. Each function has its own test file under `test/`, so a failing statistic points at one file.
4	
5	**Tech Stack:** Node.js 20 (`node:test`, `node:assert/strict`), CommonJS modules, no runtime or dev dependencies. The suite runs with `npm test`, which is `node --test`.
6	
7	These apply to every task below. They are written down once so each task can stay short on process and long on content.
8	
9	- **Module format.** CommonJS (`require` / `module.exports`). `package.json` has no `type` field, and this plan never adds one.
10	- **Test files.** One file per function, named `test/<functionName>.test.js`, using `const { test } = require('node:test');` and `const assert = require('node:assert/strict');`. Test names are full sentences in the present tense that say what the function does ("counts hyphenated compounds as one word"), never "test 1".
11	- **Red before green.** Every task writes its test file first, runs `npm test`, and sees it fail for the stated reason before any implementation is written. A test that has never failed has not shown that it can.
12	- **Argument validation.** Text arguments must be strings. A non-string throws `TypeError` whose message starts with the function name and a colon. Numeric arguments that are out of range throw `RangeError` with the same prefix. Tests assert on the error class and on the message prefix, never on the full message text.
13	- **No state.** None of the functions mutates its arguments, caches results, or reads anything from the environment. Calling a function twice with the same arguments returns equal values.
14	- **Commits.** One commit per task, conventional prefix `feat:`, message in the imperative, and the test file and implementation in the same commit. Do not commit while `npm test` is red.
15	- **Scope.** English prose only. Right-to-left scripts, languages without spaces between words, and markup stripping are out of scope; the notes in each task name the specific cases that are deliberately left alone.
16	
17	## Task Dependency Order
18	
19	Tasks run in order. Task 1 introduces `tokenize`, which Task 2 (the "does this segment hold a word" test), Task 3 (the word list) and Task 4 (via `wordCount`) all rely on. Task 4 depends on `wordCount` directly. No task edits the tests of an earlier task, and no task rewrites the code of an earlier task: each one only appends a function and widens the export line.

### Spec Compliance

- ✅ Spec compliant. The diff matches the brief file by file.
  - `src/textstats.js` replaces the export line and adds `DEFAULT_WORDS_PER_MINUTE` and `readingTimeMinutes` (diff lines 28-49). The code is identical to the brief's Step 3.
  - `test/readingTimeMinutes.test.js` is new and identical to the brief's Step 1. It has 10 tests.
  - `assertText` runs before the wpm check, so the text is validated first.
  - `wpm` defaults to 200 when omitted or `undefined`.
  - The wpm check rejects non-numbers, `NaN`, the infinities, zero and negatives. Fractional rates pass.
  - Both error messages start with `readingTimeMinutes:`.

  - The report says 46 tests where the brief expected 38. The brief's own count of 28 earlier tests looks stale. The controller should confirm the earlier test files contain 36 tests and that nothing outside Task 4 was added. This diff touches only the two Task 4 files.

### Strengths
- The change is purely additive. The only edit to existing code is widening the export line, and no earlier task's code or tests were rewritten.
- The implementation reuses `wordCount`, so the rate and the word count cannot disagree.
- The boundary tests (200, 201 and 400 words) use a `words(n)` helper, so they don't depend on particular prose.
- The error tests assert on the error class and the message prefix, as the global constraints require.

None.

None.

5	
6	# Subagent-Driven Development
7	
8	Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.
9	
10	**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.
11	
12	**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration
13	
14	**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
15	ledger and the tool results carry the record.
16	
17	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for anything you write to your human partner in this skill: the pre-flight question, an escalation, a BLOCKED hand-back.
18	
19	**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. While the plan has tasks left, a turn ends in exactly three cases: a BLOCKED status you cannot resolve; a question only your human partner can answer, asked in that message (ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress is such a question); or, on a harness that cannot wait in the foreground, tracked work still running, named in that message. A message that names your next step is followed by that step's tool call in the same turn. "Tasks 1 and 2 are done. Moving to Task 3." followed by a turn end is a stop: your human partner reads it as work in progress, and nothing resumes it until they type. Completing the last task does not end the plan: it opens the final whole-branch review, and the plan ends only after Finish. Each permitted turn end, and "your human partner asked you to stop", is written to the ledger in the same message that ends the turn: run `scripts/sdd-state handback PLAN_FILE --reason "<why>"` (add `--session <sid>` on a harness without `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`; `busy` or `error` is retried, and without the line the guard falls back to reading your last message). Write that line only for a question only your human partner can answer, a BLOCKED report, or their request to stop; finishing the tasks is never a reason for it. On Claude Code the SDD stop guard refuses a turn end it can prove is premature, two consecutive attempts per plan, the count resetting after any allow, with this message: "SDD stop guard: plan <plan path> is not finished (<state>; nothing tracked is live). Take the next step now, in this turn. If you are handing back to your human partner (a question only they can answer, a BLOCKED report, or they asked you to stop), run scripts/sdd-state handback PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --reason "<why>" and end the turn with that message." (with a live job the first sentences name the job and say to watch it with `tracked-job wait`). When you meet it, take the next step; writing a question you do not need answered to get past it is the stop it exists to prevent, and the log records every allow. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.
20	
21	**Tracked work only:** anything that outlives one tool call starts through your harness's tracked background option (`run_in_background` on Claude Code); never start it with a trailing `&`, `nohup`, `setsid`, `disown`, or a script that detaches a process. The harness never reports on such a process, so nothing wakes you when it ends, and a turn you end to wait for it does not resume.
22	
23	**After every context compaction:** this file fits within the 20,000 characters Claude Code re-attaches, so the copy you hold is whole. A step file you read before the compaction does not survive it. Before your next action, print the board and the ledger lines the step table names (your task's and your Setup's, never the whole ledger), find your step in the table, and Read that step file in full.
24	
25	## When to Use
26	
27	```dot
28	digraph when_to_use {

30	    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
31	    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];

37	    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
38	    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];

43	```
44	
45	**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
46	- Same session (no context switch)
47	- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
48	- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
49	- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)
50	
51	## The Process
52	
53	Each step's full text is in its own file beside this one. Read a step's file when you enter the step; after a compaction, the step table below names the one to read.
54	
55	1. **Setup** ([setup.md](setup.md)): sync the state branch and find the plan's workspace, settle where the work happens (hyperpowers:using-git-worktrees), create or read the ledger and append your session line, verify, read the plan and the spec, run the pre-flight scan. Setup's last action appends `session <sid>: setup complete`.
56	2. **Take a task and dispatch** ([task-loop.md](task-loop.md)): `scripts/sdd-state next` offers a task; claim the first and switch to its branch (none to take, or blocked: post, print the board, hand back). Dispatch the implementer, answer its questions, handle its report.
57	3. **Review the task** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): generate the review package and dispatch the task reviewer. Blocking findings go to step 4; a finding that conflicts with the plan text goes to your human partner first.
58	4. **Fix loop** ([fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md)): fix rounds, each with a scoped re-review, under the shared cap in the rules below. When no finding is left open, go back to review-and-complete.md for the gate.
59	5. **Codex task gate and completion** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): unless the task's effective tier is low, run the per-task Codex gate (blocking findings re-enter step 4). Append the `approved` line, merge back, detach, delete the task branch, and run `scripts/sdd-state complete`; any status but `complete` stops. Then step 2.
60	6. **Final review and Finish** ([final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md)): when no task remains, claim the final train, dispatch the final reviewer (one fix dispatch, one scoped re-review), the decision extractor and the Codex final gate, delete the workspace, then use hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.
61	
62	## After a compaction: the step table
63	
64	Print the board (`scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE`) and the ledger lines of your task and your Setup (`grep -E '^(Task <N>:|session <sid>: setup complete)' <workspace>/progress.md`, leaving out `Task <N>:` when you hold no task); `scripts/sdd-dir PLAN_FILE` prints the workspace. Do not Read the whole ledger after a compaction: it grows with the plan. A row's newest line is the newest of your task's lines the table names (its branch, base, implementer identity, `report`, `review`, Codex gate round, `approved`, `merged` and `fix round` lines); a line it does not name, such as a deferred minor or the gate directory, leaves your step unchanged. Then Read the step file this table names:
65	
66	| State | Step file |
67	|---|---|
68	| no ledger in the workspace, or no `setup complete` line of this session in it | [setup.md](setup.md) |
69	| the board shows no task held by this session and a task without a completion line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
70	| the held task's newest line is its branch, base, implementer identity or `report` line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
71	| its newest line is a `review` or Codex gate line approving it, an `approved` line or a `merged` line | [review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md) |
72	| its newest line is a `fix round` line, or a `review` or Codex gate line with blocking findings | [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) |
73	| this session holds the final claim, or every task has a completion line | [final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md) |
74	
75	A state the table does not cover reads [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), and you record that in the ledger.
76	
77	The table reads these ledger lines, so write each one where its step says:
78	
79	- `session <sid>: setup complete`, Setup's last action;
80	- `Task <N>: report <status> <one line>`, after an implementer's report;
81	- `Task <N>: review <approved|blocking> <reviewer id> <one line>`, after a task review or scoped re-review;
82	- `Task <N>: codex gate round <R> <approved|blocking> <one line>`, after each per-task Codex gate round.
83	
84	## Rules for every step
85	
86	These hold in every step file. Where a step file and this section differ, this section governs.
87	
88	- Tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE — do not re-dispatch them. Conversation memory does not survive compaction. After compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
89	- Dispatch implementer, task-reviewer, fix-round, re-review and final-reviewer subagents with `run_in_background: false`. Your next step always depends on the result, and a foreground call keeps your turn open, which is what an editor such as Zed shows as the session working. A background dispatch ends the turn while the subagent runs, and the editor shows the session idle.
90	- Run a covering command expected to finish within 10 minutes in the foreground, with an explicit timeout of at least its expected runtime and at most 600000 ms. A command that may run past 10 minutes is a tracked job; [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), "Waiting on subagents and long commands", gives its commands and watch budget.
91	- One implementer at a time in this session: parallel work is other sessions' (one controller per task branch); never dispatch two implementers at once here.
92	- Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review. The one exception is the de-minimis fix in [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md).
93	- The task reviewer's blocking findings and the per-task Codex gate's blocking findings form one loop with ONE shared cap of **five rounds per task**: the gate does not run a count of its own.
94	- When round 5's re-review — or a per-task Codex gate at the spent cap — still leaves blocking findings open, stop dispatching and surface the task as BLOCKED, as [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) describes under the breaker.
95	
96	## Model Selection
97	
98	Match the model to the task's difficulty rather than defaulting. Two rules are
99	defaults you will get wrong by omission, so they stay here: **always specify
100	the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent** — an omitted model inherits
101	your session's, usually the most capable and most expensive — and **a mid-tier
102	model is the floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose
103	descriptions**, whatever the schedule pressure. The cheapest tier is for
104	transcription, where the task's own text carries the complete code to write,
105	and for single-file mechanical fixes. The per-role guidance, the complexity
106	signals, and the fix-loop escalation rule are in
107	[model-selection.md](model-selection.md).
108	
109	## The waiting board
110	
111	Before you ask your human partner a question, hand back BLOCKED, meet an
112	empty frontier (`held` or `blocked`), or stop on a merge conflict, post what
113	you wait on: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --kind
114	<question|tasks|merge|gate|handoff> [--task N] --note "<one line>"`, and put
115	the session lines of `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE` in what you write.
116	When you resume, clear it: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --clear`.
117	The board is how your human partner finds the session that needs them among
118	several; a session that holds a claim and posts nothing shows as quiet
119	after half an hour, which is where they look for a permission prompt.
120	
121	## Risk Tiers (per-task Codex gate applicability)
122	
123	Tiers are `low`, `standard`, `high`, declared per task in the plan. A task
124	skips the per-task Codex gate only when all three hold: declared low, the
125	plan's own Codex gate actually reviewed the plan, and no escalation trigger
126	fired at any point during execution. That skip is recorded durably. An
127	unreviewed low tier — plan gate skipped, degraded, or outcome unknown —
128	executes as standard, and a task demoted that way runs the full train and
129	records NO tier-skip event. The Claude task reviewer and the final
130	whole-branch train never tier off. When any task did skip, write
131	`tier-skips.md` in this plan's workspace; Final Review hands its path to the
132	final reviewer and the final Codex gate. The escalation triggers, the
133	fallback rules, and the exact ledger line shape are in
134	[risk-tiers.md](risk-tiers.md) — read it before dispatching any task declared
135	low.
136	
137	## Common Rationalizations
138	
139	The excuses that show up mid-run and what is actually true:
140	[common-rationalizations.md](common-rationalizations.md). Read it the moment you
141	catch yourself justifying a shortcut.
142	
143	## Example Workflow
144	
145	A complete worked run, dispatch through finish:
146	[example-workflow.md](example-workflow.md).
